message.content:
Search this repository thoroughly for how webhook delivery workers consume work. Specifically:
1. Find any webhook delivery worker code — grep for "webhook" combined with "worker", "consumer", "delivery", "queue", "broker"
2. Check if NATS or RabbitMQ is used anywhere: grep for "nats", "rabbitmq", "amqp", "NATS", "RabbitMQ", "AMQP"
3. Look for how webhook jobs are enqueued and dequeued — grep for "queue", "enqueue", "dequeue", "job", "bull", "bullmq", "pgboss", "pg-boss", "graphile", "trigger"
4. Check for any PostgreSQL-based queue mechanism (LISTEN/NOTIFY, SKIP LOCKED, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)

Be very thorough — search across the entire repo. Report exact file paths and line numbers.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

86	// TestPostSignsRequest verifies the end-to-end Standard Webhooks signature so a
87	// receiver following the documented verification recipe will accept our requests.
88	func TestPostSignsRequest(t *testing.T) {
89		// httptest listens on 127.0.0.1, which the SSRF guard blocks by default.
90		prev := AllowPrivateIPs
91		AllowPrivateIPs = true
92		defer func() { AllowPrivateIPs = prev }()
93	
94		rawKey := []byte("0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef")
95		cases := []struct {
96			name   string
97			secret string
98			key    []byte
99		}{
100			{name: "plain secret", secret: "plain-secret-value", key: []byte("plain-secret-value")},
101			{name: "whsec_ secret", secret: "whsec_" + base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(rawKey), key: rawKey},
102		}
103	
104		for _, tc := range cases {
105			t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
106				var gotID, gotTimestamp, gotSignature string
107				var gotBody []byte
108				server := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
109					gotID = r.Header.Get("webhook-id")
110					gotTimestamp = r.Header.Get("webhook-timestamp")
111					gotSignature = r.Header.Get("webhook-signature")
112					gotBody, _ = io.ReadAll(r.Body)
113					_, _ = w.Write([]byte(`{"code":0}`))
114				}))
115				defer server.Close()
116	
117				err := Post(&WebhookRequestPayload{
118					URL:           server.URL,
119					ActivityType:  "memos.memo.created",
120					Creator:       "users/1",
121					SigningSecret: tc.secret,
122				})
123				require.NoError(t, err)
124	
125				require.True(t, strings.HasPrefix(gotID, "msg_"), "webhook-id should be prefixed with msg_")
126				require.NotEmpty(t, gotTimestamp)
127				require.True(t, strings.HasPrefix(gotSignature, "v1,"), "signature should carry the v1 version tag")
128	
129				// Recompute the signature the way a receiver would and confirm it matches.
130				mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, tc.key)
131				mac.Write([]byte(gotID + "." + gotTimestamp + "."))
132				mac.Write(gotBody)
133				want := base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil))
134				require.Equal(t, "v1,"+want, gotSignature)
135			})
136		}
137	}

content.text:
Here is my complete report on how webhook delivery workers consume work in this repository.

---

## Findings

### 1. Webhook Delivery Worker Architecture

This project (Memos, a note-taking app) uses a simple **in-process Go channel-based queue** with goroutine workers for webhook delivery. There is no external message broker or job queue system.

**Core file:** `/bench/repo/internal/webhook/webhook.go`

The entire worker pool is set up in an `init()` function at lines 42-55:

```go
var asyncPostQueue = make(chan *WebhookRequestPayload, 128)

func init() {
    for range 4 {
        go func() {
            for payload := range asyncPostQueue {
                if err := Post(payload); err != nil {
                    slog.Warn("Failed to dispatch webhook asynchronously",
                        slog.String("url", payload.URL),
                        slog.String("activityType", payload.ActivityType),
                        slog.Any("err", err))
                }
            }
        }()
    }
}
```

Key characteristics:
- **4 goroutine workers** are spawned at process startup (line 43).
- They consume from a **buffered Go channel** (`asyncPostQueue`) with capacity **128** (line 39).
- Each worker loops over the channel, calling `Post()` synchronously for each payload.
- Errors are logged but not retried -- failed deliveries are silently dropped after logging.

### 2. How Webhook Jobs Are Enqueued

**Enqueue function:** `PostAsync()` at lines 184-196 of `/bench/repo/internal/webhook/webhook.go`:

```go
func PostAsync(requestPayload *WebhookRequestPayload) {
    if requestPayload == nil {
        slog.Warn("Dropped webhook dispatch because payload is nil")
        return
    }
    select {
    case asyncPostQueue <- requestPayload:
    default:
        slog.Warn("Dropped webhook dispatch because the async queue is full", ...)
    }
}
```

Key characteristics:
- Uses a **non-blocking send** via `select`/`default` -- if the channel is full (128 items), the webhook is **silently dropped** (with a log warning).
- No persistence, no retry, no dead-letter mechanism.

**Call sites that enqueue webhooks:**

All in `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go`:
- `dispatchMemoRelatedWebhook()` (line 71) -- calls `webhook.PostAsync(payload)` for each of the user's webhooks.
- `DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook()` (line 43) -- same pattern.

These dispatch functions are triggered from:
- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go` line 157 -- on memo creation (`DispatchMemoCreatedWebhook`)
- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go` line 562 -- on memo deletion (`DispatchMemoDeletedWebhook`)
- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_update_helpers.go` line 67 -- on memo update (`DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook`)
- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service_comments.go` line 119 -- on comment creation (`DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook`)

### 3. NATS / RabbitMQ / AMQP: NOT USED

Grep results across the entire repository for `nats`, `rabbitmq`, `amqp`, `NATS`, `RabbitMQ`, `AMQP` returned only one false-positive hit in a Catalan locale file (`/bench/repo/web/src/locales/ca.json`) where the word "eliminats" contains the substring "nats". No actual NATS, RabbitMQ, or AMQP client library, configuration, or code exists anywhere in the codebase. None of these appear in `go.mod` or `go.sum`.

### 4. External Job Queue Libraries: NOT USED

No hits for: `bull`, `bullmq`, `pgboss`, `pg-boss`, `graphile`, `celery`, `sidekiq`, `resque`, `faktory`, `machinery`, `asynq`, `river`, `que`, `delayed_job`, or `redis` in `go.mod` or any application code.

### 5. PostgreSQL-Based Queue Mechanisms: NOT USED

No hits for `LISTEN`, `NOTIFY`, `SKIP LOCKED`, or `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` in any `.go` or `.sql` file.

### 6. Webhook Storage

Webhooks were originally stored in a dedicated `webhook` database table (created in migration `0.18`). This table was **dropped** in migration `0.25` across all three supported databases:
- `/bench/repo/store/migration/sqlite/0.25/00__remove_webhook.sql`
- `/bench/repo/store/migration/postgres/0.25/00__remove_webhook.sql`
- `/bench/repo/store/migration/mysql/0.25/00__remove_webhook.sql`

Webhooks are now stored as **user settings** (protobuf-serialized `WebhooksUserSetting` within the `user_setting` table), managed by methods in `/bench/repo/store/user_setting.go` (lines 311-417): `GetUserWebhooks`, `AddUserWebhook`, `RemoveUserWebhook`, `UpdateUserWebhook`.

### 7. Related: Internal Cron Scheduler

The project includes a cron-based scheduler at `/bench/repo/internal/scheduler/scheduler.go`, but it is **not used for webhook delivery**. There are no references to the scheduler package from `server/` or `cmd/` code. The scheduler appears to be a general-purpose utility that is not yet wired into the main application.

### 8. Related: Email Async Queue (Same Pattern)

The email package at `/bench/repo/internal/email/email.go` uses the exact same architectural pattern -- a buffered channel of capacity 128 with 2 goroutine workers, fire-and-forget with drop-on-full semantics.

---

## Summary

The webhook delivery system is entirely **in-process** with no external dependencies. It uses a Go buffered channel (`chan *WebhookRequestPayload`, capacity 128) as the queue, with 4 goroutine workers consuming from it in a loop. Jobs are enqueued via `PostAsync()` with non-blocking semantics (payloads are dropped if the queue is full). There is no persistence, retry logic, dead-letter queue, or external message broker (no NATS, RabbitMQ, Redis, or PostgreSQL-based queue mechanism). The HTTP POST to the webhook URL has a 30-second timeout and includes SSRF protection against private IP addresses.
